title: Certificates: a strength-4 partly cyclic covering perfect hash family, CA(7031233; 4, 100000, 25)
body:
This pull request adds one covering perfect hash family of strength 4 found by our search, CPHF(18; 100000, 25, 4). It gives CA(7031233; 4, 100000, 25), N = 18(25^4 - 1) + 1. The table has no strength-4 row past 10,000 columns yet. The family is partly cyclic (`builds_on` cphf-smc2006;pcphf-c2026): 14 of its 18 rows are progressions u_(c+1) = M u_c. Eight multiply by a primitive element of GF(25^4); three are affine powers a^j in GF(25^3); three are (b^j, j) in GF(25^2) x GF(25). The other 4 rows are random; the last of them was repaired by local search. It stays below your PCT line at 100,000 columns (7,421,856).

**Your CI.** fastprog stops at 65,535 columns, so the planner should use `progression`. Your unit costs give about 2.1 core-hours for the hashing with the factor 2, plus about 1.1 for the shift tests: 142,068 representatives, each shifted across the columns and tested in the other rows. Your tools/check_submission.py passes locally: estimate in 1 shard, 2.07 core-hours with the factor 2; enters as VERIFIED.

**Checks so far.** Two exact checks pass, each counting all 1.67e14 triples {0, x, y, z}: our refinement checker t4ref and your cphfcheck in progression mode, run locally (4.17e18 t-sets covered, 0 uncovered). Our separately written cells checker, t4cells, is still running at this width; I will add its result here when it finishes. Your certificate workflow's check after the merge is the binding one. title: Certificates: a strength-6 covering perfect hash family with q = 8 to 3,171 columns, CA(6029136; 6, 3171, 8)
body:
This pull request adds one Sherwood covering perfect hash family of strength 6, SCPHF(23; 3171, 8, 6), which gives CA(6029136; 6, 3171, 8) (6,029,136 = 23(8^6 - 8) + 8).

**What it lowers.** 1,171 cells at strength 6 with v = 8, k = 2,001 to 3,171 (up to k = 2,000 the table's CA(4980592; 6, 2000, 8) is smaller). The table's best there today comes from the November 2024 tables:

| k | best known now | from |
|---|---|---|
| 2,001 to 2,067 | 21,757,869 | Power N-CT53^2T14 |
| 2,068 to 2,226 | 21,987,217 | Power N-CT53^2T11 |
| 2,227 to 2,385 | 22,015,889 | Power N-CT53^2T8 |
| 2,386 to 2,438 | 22,019,473 | Power N-CT53^2T7 |
| 2,439 to 2,491 | 22,019,921 | Power N-CT53^2T6 |
| 2,492 to 2,810 | 22,020,012 | Power N-CT53^2+1 |
| 2,811 to 2,851 | 23,592,331 | Power N-CT73^2T27S12 |
| 2,852 to 2,912 | 23,592,779 | Power N-CT73^2T26S12 |
| 2,913 to 3,171 | 23,592,870 | Power N-CT73^2T19S12 (row k = 3,345) |

In the derived lookup the best at these k is 11,160,079, from fusing one symbol of CA(11160081; 6, 3950, 9) (#41). 6,029,136 is below both.

**The file.** Every row is an affine progression (23 of 23): row r is j -> a_r^j for an element a_r of GF(8^5). It comes from the pure cyclic mode of cphf6c_v2.c (public, MIT), which does no search, so it reruns byte for byte. The program draws 4,600 columns; this family is the first 3,171 of them.

**Our checks.** Every set of six columns was checked exactly twice, on our coding:
- by scphf6_fast.c on the whole 4,600-column draw. It found nine sets holding column 0 that no row covers, the least with largest column 3,171 ({0, 453, 1510, 1661, 2718, 3171}). Since the rows are progressions, every uncovered set is a shift of one of these, so none lies within the first 3,171 columns;
- by fullcheck6.c, a second checker written separately, in mode full on the 3,171 columns: all 4,199,552,135,592 steps of its plan, nothing uncovered.

Both logs are public at github.com/arhancanli/quantavane-covering-arrays (record/q8_n23_k4600/ and checks/second/q8_3171_combine.txt).

**The conversion.** Our GF(8) is GF(2)[x]/(x^3 + x + 1) with the codes c0 + 2 c1 + 4 c2. That is the Conway coding, so for q = 8 the field map of our converter is the identity, and the file writes each point P as the vector (1, P), the integer 32768 + P (checked on all 72,933 entries). The same rule gave table/certificates/CPHF_19_2000_8_6.txt, which your check passed. (Where a field map is needed, it keeps coverage: an isomorphism sends each 6 x 6 determinant to the image of that determinant, so zero stays zero and nonzero stays nonzero.) On this file, in the Conway field, our own code found:
- all 23 rows are affine progressions (one map per row, checked on every column);
- 10,000,000 random sets of six columns, and every 6-set of 20 random 30-column windows (11,875,500 sets), are covered;
- 500 random sets of six columns show all 262,144 tuples in the expanded array;
- checker/cphf_conway_check.py (public, exact in the Conway field) finds nothing uncovered in 5 more random 30-column windows.

Red controls: converted the same way, the first 3,172 columns leave {0, 453, 1510, 1661, 2718, 3171} uncovered in all 23 rows (cphf_conway_check.py finds it too, in a window that holds it), and in the converted 4,600-column draw, eight of the first check's nine base sets, each at four shifts (32 sets), stay uncovered. To show that these checks see a wrong field, we read the files in the other cubic field, GF(2)[y]/(y^3 + y^2 + 1). Without an isomorphism no row is a progression and all 32 sets come out covered. With the isomorphism x -> y + 1, all 23 rows are progressions and the 32 sets are uncovered again. Random sets of six columns were covered in both cases, so they cannot catch a wrong field on their own.

**CI cost (our estimate).** fullcheck6 checked every base set in 10.7 hours on 4 CPUs, about 43 core-hours. With the factor of 2 that is about 86 core-hours, 5 shards of at most 5 hours, well inside the budget of 400 core-hours. The plan your check prints on this pull request gives the exact figure. The array has about 1.9 x 10^10 entries, under 10^12, so it is also hashed.

Released under CC BY 4.0 (Rule 4). mode `auto`, builds_on `cphf-smc2006;new doi:10.5281/zenodo.23839216`; HOW.md gives the program and its arguments.

title: Certificates: fused listings, tests of alphabets above 25, the derived ladder past 100,000 columns
body:
This pull request contains the three commits offered in #54, one for each of its questions. Each one works without the others, so any of them can be taken alone, or none.

1. **f1dab7e: fused listings.** `certificates.csv` may end with a column `expansion`. When that column is empty, nothing changes. A rule with fusing steps, such as `smc-1-affine+fuse2 6`, makes the claim a fused listing: the array that a family already in the table gives at a smaller alphabet (Lemma 3.1 of Colbourn, Keri, Rivas Soriano and Schlage-Puchta 2010). The claim names the family by its file in `table/certificates/`, and `mode` stays empty. The family is not checked again: the row stands on the family's exact check and the lemma, and carries the stamp of that check, as your listings of CPHF_16_781_5_6.txt do. On main, one job rebuilds the array as a stream (`cphfcheck expand`, then the new `tools/cphf/fusestream.c`), hashes it and spot-checks 10,000 random t-sets. The listing enters CERTIFICATES.csv beside the family's own and uses the family's file. fusestream gives the same bytes as fuse2.c, and it rebuilds both of your fused listings to their array_sha256.
2. **a59f9d8: alphabets above 25.** The checker needs no change: cphfcheck.c already builds every field up to q = 32 from the Conway polynomials, and check_certificates.py takes v up to 32. The commit adds tests, and adds a note to rungs at a strength and alphabet that have no baseline. Today every (t, v) has baseline rows, so the page is unchanged.
3. **cae1663: strength 3 past 100,000 columns.** Nothing in the checker depends on 100,000. derive_table.py continues its ladder past 100,000 only up to the widest counted entry of a strength, so derived.csv and both pages are unchanged until such an entry exists.

What it adds: no rows. Commit 1 is what lets fused listings enter later.

What it costs on GitHub: the consistency check and the self-test, as for any change to tools/. No certificate work runs. A fused listing submitted later costs no exact check and one job, which takes about 10 ns per entry of the array: 2 to 30 minutes for the arrays in view.

- **Companion preprint & standalone verifier (Zenodo, CC BY 4.0):** Kevin Grey, *"Improved Upper Bounds for Strength-3 Covering Arrays over Six Symbols via Mixed Short and Regular PSL(2, 5) Orbits"* (2 Nov 2026), https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23877721 (concept DOI `10.5281/zenodo.23877720`), including all 11 Table 2 starters for `CA(456; 3, 12, 6)` and the 10-starter `PSL(2, 5)` seeds at `k = 10, 11` in `verify_covering_arrays.py` (also noting primary-source credit to `ck-ck2002`, `sa-ccl2008`, and Sarkar–Colbourn 2017 `doi:10.1137/16M1067767` Theorem 8 for binary arrays on symbol pairs).
- Identifying `{0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5}` with `P^1(F_5) = {0, 1, 2, 3, 4, inf}` (`5 <-> inf`), `PSL(2, 5) = <T, S>` (order 60, generated on `{0..5}` by the one-line image tuples `(g(0),...,g(5))` `T = (1,2,3,4,0,5)` [`z -> z+1 mod 5`, `5 -> 5`] and `S = (5,4,2,3,1,0)` [`z -> -1/z mod 5`, `0 <-> 5`]) partitions `{0..5}^3` into 1 constant orbit (size 6), 3 two-symbol orbits (size 30), and 2 all-distinct orbits (size 60). - **`CA(366; 3, 10, 6)`** and **`CA(418; 3, 11, 6)`** start from mixed-`(30, 60)` `PSL(2, 5)` orbit seeds — a pure `396`-row `PSL(2, 5)` orbit cover at `k = 10`, and a `426`-row `PSL(2, 5)` orbit union (`11` of `825` non-constant target orbits uncovered, repaired to a `426`-row covering array via single-cell tabu moves) at `k = 11` — followed by iterative row deletion with Nurmela-style tabu single-cell post-optimization. `builds_on`: `ck-cck1999;pgl-macc2018;tabu-n2004;postop-nck2013;new https://github.com/chrispbsmolen/ca-tools/issues/19`.

title: Eight strength-4 covering arrays improving the table (CA(4,100,3), CA(4,105,3), CA(4,7,5), CA(4,8,5), CA(4,7,6), CA(4,8,6), CA(4,12,6), CA(4,26,6))
body:
Eight explicit strength-4 covering arrays, each improving the best known size in the table (re-checked against upstream 392d8c9 on 2026-10-30):

| Parameters | Previous best | New N |
|---|---|---|
| CA(N; 4, 100, 3) | 645 | 633 |
| CA(N; 4, 105, 3) | 657 | 644 |
| CA(N; 4, 7, 5) | 910 | 825 |
| CA(N; 4, 8, 5) | 1125 | 1050 |
| CA(N; 4, 7, 6) | 1844 | 1832 |
| CA(N; 4, 8, 6) | 1975 | 1963 |
| CA(N; 4, 12, 6) | 3944 | 3942 |
| CA(N; 4, 26, 6) | 6456 | 6445 |

Three arrays first submitted here, CA(3568; 4, 9, 7), CA(4202; 4, 16, 6) and CA(6581; 4, 27, 6), were withdrawn on 2026-10-31: the deposit of Bai XunDi (doi:10.5281/zenodo.23787055, pull requests #9 and following) has smaller arrays.

By stair-step, CA(633; 4, 100, 3) also improves k = 95..99 and CA(644; 4, 105, 3) improves k = 101..104. The superseded intermediate arrays CA(636; 4, 100, 3) and CA(908; 4, 7, 5) were removed from the folder.

Methods:
- CA(825; 4, 7, 5) and CA(1050; 4, 8, 5): unions of cosets of a linear [k, 2] code over GF(5) whose generator has rank 2 on every 4 columns, the shifts chosen by local search so that every 4-set of columns sees all 25 cosets of the projected code (33 and 42 cosets). The program was written by Claude Opus for k = 7; the k = 8 array came from the same program with k as a parameter.
- The other six: post-optimisation of the table's own record arrays (row deletion, then local re-assignment of non-essential entries), with C search programs written by Claude Opus. For CA(4,7,6), CA(4,8,6) and CA(4,26,6) this was repeated from each previous array (1844 -> 1838 -> 1833 -> 1832, 1975 -> 1966 -> 1963, 6456 -> 6453 -> 6451 -> 6445); the intermediate arrays and every step's program are in the repository.

Arrays, programs and a verification script: https://github.com/tns-research/covering-array-records (release v1.3, doi:10.5281/zenodo.23741408). `tools/check_submission.py` passes locally on all eleven files (`exceeds_table`).

Credit: T. N. Sitjar (tns-research).
